The raw government corpus contains inherent source biases that impact retrieval:
Uneven Service Coverage.
Frequently transacted procedures dominate the text, yield-
ing vastly more usable chunks, whereas uncommon procedural exceptions possess little
usable evidence
Formal Institutional Language.
Official phrasing heavily overrides local spelling
variants, mixed-language terminology, and colloquial inquiries.
Time and Versioning Biases.
Legacy versions of the charter contain outdated fees,
timelines, and office locations. Superseded versions are explicitly isolated from the active
answer corpus but retained in a change log.
To mitigate digitization failures, the text extraction pipeline applies the following controls:
Artifact Removal.
Machine-readable text is extracted, and OCR is applied to scanned
pages. Repeated headers, page artifacts, and accidental whitespace are stripped, while
critical procedural conditions, numerical figures, negation terms, and units are strictly
preserved.
Tabular Integrity Verification.
Procedural tables detailing rows, processing fees,
required documents, and turnaround times are cross-checked manually against the original
page images. Extraction mistakes are corrected directly; the system strictly forbids the
use of an LLM to hallucinate or reconstruct missing text.
Deduplication.
Duplicate passages are removed while retaining their source links.
Valid low-frequency exceptions are preserved; the pipeline explicitly avoids discarding
valid official material simply to equalize the number of chunks per service category.
The cleaned text must be segmented into source-linked chunks that preserve proce-
dural context while conforming to the dense embedding model’s architectural constraints.
Because the paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2 model imposes a default 128-
token sequence limit, chunk boundaries are defined by actual token lengths rather than
arbitrary character counts to prevent unnoticed truncation of critical policy data during
vectorization. Specifically, the corpus is segmented into uniform chunks of 120 tokens with
a 20-token overlap using a HuggingFace tokenizer-aware splitter, preserving procedural
continuity across chunk boundaries.
The system does not employ synthetic feature generation or random oversam-
pling of official passages to balance the database as this architecture performs Retrieval-
Augmented Generation rather than supervised classification. Instead, structural imbal-
ance is addressed through stratified query selection during evaluation. The system eval-
uation benchmark enforces an equal quota of underlying scenario questions across all
target services, ensuring that high-volume administrative categories do not skew the final
performance metrics.

3.2.3
Pre-Retrieval Query Normalization Pipeline
The primary novel architectural contribution of this study is the pre-retrieval query
normalization pipeline. The pipeline receives the raw code-switched citizen query from the
web interface, processes it through three sequential sub-modules, then outputs a normal-
ized English query to the hybrid retrieval engine. The three sub-modules are: dictionary-
assisted lexical injection, constrained LLM query translation, and the ambiguity fallback
mechanism.
Dictionary-Assisted Lexical Injection
Upon receiving the citizen’s raw Bislish or Taglish query, the system performs a
map lookup against the constructed dictionary. The lookup operation scans the query
for tokens that match entries in the dictionary’s key set.
For each recognized term,
the system retrieves the corresponding verified English definition and injects it explicitly
into the large language model (LLM) translation prompt as contextual grounding. The
injection process prevents the LLM from applying probabilistic guessing or pattern-based
hallucination to resolve ambiguous dialect vocabulary during translation. The mechanism
directly operationalizes the dictionary-assisted augmentation methodology [19].
Constrained LLM Query Translation
The dictionary-augmented query, now enriched with injected English term defini-
tions, is passed to the Mistral 7B language model. The translation is executed using a
few-shot prompt that includes one to two examples of correctly translated Bislish gover-
nance inquiries paired with their formal English equivalents. The translation output is
strictly constrained to a maximum of 150 tokens through a hard generation length limit
applied. This constraint directly addresses the overgeneration failure mode documented
by Miranda et al. [20] wherein LLMs produce verbose and incoherent outputs on short
conversational inputs when no generation length ceiling is enforced. It accommodates the
complete English translation of a typical single-sentence citizen inquiry while physically
preventing the model from appending unprompted additional text. The resulting formal
English query is then submitted to the hybrid retrieval engine.
Ambiguity Fallback Mechanism
If the dictionary lookup finds two or more conflicting term mappings for the same
input token, this shows a high-ambiguity case. In such situations, the system cannot
confidently determine the citizen’s intended meaning. The pipeline then activates the
ambiguity fallback mechanism before any translation or retrieval takes place. The system
returns a structured clarifying prompt to the citizen interface, displaying the conflicting
interpretations in the format: Did you mean [Term A] or [Term B]? The citizen’s selection
is then processed as a new, unambiguous input to the normalization pipeline. This fallback
makes sure that no low-confidence or semantically corrupted query vector gets submitted
to the FAISS dense index. This protects the factual integrity and retrieval precision of
the entire downstream pipeline [20].

3.2.4
Build the Hybrid Retrieval Index
This phase constructs the dual-index hybrid retrieval engine forming the non-
parametric memory of the RAG architecture. The system combines a sparse BM25 index
for exact lexical term matching with a dense Facebook AI Similarity Search (FAISS)
vector index for semantic intent matching. Both indices are constructed as a one-time
offline operation prior to system deployment and loaded into server memory at applica-
tion startup, guaranteeing consistent query-time retrieval latency independent of corpus
expansion.
Sparse BM25 Index Construction.
Sparse retrieval is implemented using the rank bm25
library, applying the probabilistic BM25 ranking function. BM25 scores document chunks
by weighting term frequency and inverse document frequency relative to document length
normalization. This component provides the exact lexical precision required to locate spe-
cific municipal identifiers, such as ordinance numbers, permit fees, processing timelines,
and explicit statutory clauses in the Davao City Citizens’ Charter.
Dense FAISS Vector Index Construction.
Dense semantic retrieval is implemented
using the paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2 SentenceTransformer model. All pre-
processed 120-token corpus chunks are mapped into a 384-dimensional dense vector space
using the paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2 encoder, strictly preserving the se-
quence boundary to eliminate downstream vector truncation. The resulting embeddings
are indexed using FAISS to execute approximate nearest-neighbor searches via Maximum
Inner Product Search (MIPS) or cosine distance. This dense index enables the retrieval
of semantically equivalent policy passages even when conversational citizen queries share
zero exact vocabulary with formal charter texts.
Hybrid Linear Score Fusion
Candidate passages retrieved from the sparse and dense indices are integrated using
a constrained linear combination with domain-specific keyword boosting:
FinalScore(d) = α · SBM25(d) + β · Sdense(d) + γ · Sboost(d)
(3.1)
where SBM25(d) and Sdense(d) represent Min-Max normalized retrieval scores scaled to the
interval [0, 1] across candidate passages, and Sboost(d) represents a normalized relevance
weight based on dictionary-matched terms in chunk d. The coefficients α, β, γ are subject
to the simplex constraint α + β + γ = 1.
3.2.5
Develop the LLM Generation Module
This phase configures the generative language model that synthesizes the retrieved
Citizens’ Charter context into a grounded, citizen-facing response. The generator is im-
plemented using Mistral 7B, a seven-billion-parameter open-source language model. It
was selected since it outperforms larger models, including Llama 2 13B, on reasoning and
instruction-following benchmarks relevant to structured question answering, and it is well-
suited for strict zero-shot and few-shot constrained generation due to its grouped-query
attention architecture [13].

3.2.8
Overfitting Controls and Pipeline Safeguards
To maintain scientific integrity and prevent biased performance reporting, this study
establishes explicit safeguards against machine learning misrepresentation, data leakage,
and pipeline overfitting.
Inapplicability of Supervised Neural Training Controls.
This research utilizes
pretrained transformer checkpoints operating exclusively in pure inference mode with fixed
neural weights. Because no gradient descent, backpropagation, or parameter updates are
performed, traditional neural network training controls are explicitly inapplicable to this
methodology.
Controlling Pipeline Overfitting and Data Leakage.
While model weights re-
main fixed, iterative adjustments to system components, such as tuning fusion parameters
(α, β, γ), adding dictionary entries, altering candidate pool depth L, or modifying prompt

instructions introduce severe risks of pipeline overfitting if guided by final test results. To
guarantee uncorrupted evaluation, the methodology implements a strict Grouped Devel-
opment or Held-Out Test Split Protocol:
1. Grouped Scenario Partitioning: Each scenario is formulated into three language
variants: formal English, Tagalog, and Bislish. To prevent cross-lingual data leakage
between splits, all three language variants and close paraphrases of a scenario share
a single Question-Group ID. The entire group is assigned en bloc to either the
development split or the held-out test split.
2. Dataset Allocation Rules:
Development Set: Used exclusively for system debugging, prompt engineer-
ing, dictionary entry verification, and tuning retrieval fusion weights (α, β, γ)
via grid search.
Final Held-Out Test Set: Managed under a restricted-access manifest. This
set is strictly reserved for single-pass evaluation of the frozen baseline and
proposed architectures.
3. Pipeline Freeze Point: Prior to running final test evaluations, all system components—
including the municipal dictionary, FAISS vector indices, prompt templates, can-
didate pool depth L, Top-K limits, and fusion weights (α, β, γ)—are completely
frozen under a registered configuration manifest. No dictionary entries or prompt
adjustments are added based on test set errors.
4. Deterministic Inference Safeguards: To eliminate generative stochasticity dur-
ing generation, the large language model’s temperature parameter is set to Temperature =
0. This restricts decoding to greedy token selection, ensuring that identical context-
query inputs yield fully deterministic and repeatable outputs.
5. Unfiltered Performance Reporting: All system outputs on the held-out test
set are retained and reported in full. Unfavorable test outcomes are documented as
systemic limitations rather than retroactively corrected.
